items.title: Water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius, not zero
items.claim: Cool any substance and it gets denser as it approaches freezing — except water. Water reaches maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius and then becomes LESS dense as it cools further to 0 degrees Celsius.
items.prompt: Why does ice float on liquid water?

options.text: Trapped air bubbles make ice less dense than liquid water
Hydrogen bonds force water molecules into an open hexagonal lattice on freezing, so solid water occupies about 9 percent more volume than liquid water
Ice is colder, and colder things float
Surface tension on the underside of ice holds it up

items.reveal_title: Hydrogen bonding wins over packing efficiency
items.reveal:
In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and re-form constantly, and molecules can crowd together. When water freezes, every molecule locks into a tetrahedral arrangement where each oxygen hydrogen-bonds to exactly four neighbours. That structure is open and roomy — about 9 percent more volume than the liquid.

This is why ponds freeze top-down rather than bottom-up. Fish survive winter because the densest water (4 degrees Celsius) sinks and the ice layer insulates everything below. If water behaved normally, lakes would freeze solid and life as we know it could not exist.
items.why: Students assume cooling always increases density. The hydrogen bond's geometry, not the temperature, controls the packing.

items.title: Lithium reacts less vigorously than sodium even though it is above it
items.claim: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs all react more violently with water in turn. Yet lithium has the highest ionisation energy AND the most negative standard electrode potential (-3.04 V — even more negative than caesium's -3.03 V).

options.text: Lithium is mislabelled — it should be in Group 2
Reactivity with water is rate-controlled by surface kinetics: lithium has a high melting point and forms a thick LiOH crust, so it reacts slowly even though it is highly thermodynamically active
Lithium doesn't really react with water at all
The standard electrode potential table is wrong

items.reveal:
Standard electrode potential measures the thermodynamic tendency to release electrons in aqueous solution. Lithium's small ion has very high hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs caesium's -264), which more than compensates its higher ionisation energy.

But observed reactivity also depends on how fast the metal can deliver electrons. Lithium has a higher melting point (181°C) than sodium (98°C), so it does not melt in the heat of its own reaction with water. The LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms an adherent coating. So lithium fizzes calmly; sodium spits and ignites.

Down the group, melting points drop, hydroxides become more soluble, and surface kinetics dominate.
items.why: Reactivity series is often presented as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force AND a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Atomic radius goes UP across the lanthanides (then drops)
items.claim: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period: protons increase but the outer shell is the same. The 4f electrons in the lanthanides screen the nucleus so poorly that radius decreases throughout the row — and then the 5d and 6s elements after them are SMALLER than expected.
items.prompt: What's the consequence of this 'lanthanide contraction'?

options.text: Elements just after the lanthanides (Hf, Ta, W and below) have surprisingly small radii, almost identical to those of the elements above them in the same group (Zr, Nb, Mo) — so zirconium and hafnium have nearly identical chemistry and are very hard to separate
Atomic radius goes UP, not down, across the lanthanides

items.reveal:
Across the 14 lanthanides, atomic number rises by 14 but the added electrons go into 4f orbitals, which are 'inside' the 6s shell and screen the outer electrons very poorly. So the effective nuclear charge felt by the 6s shell grows steadily — the outer shell shrinks.

By the time you reach hafnium (Z=72, just after the lanthanides), the atomic radius is approximately the same as zirconium (Z=40) above it. Atomic radius is 159 pm for Zr, 156 pm for Hf — virtually identical.

The practical consequence: Zr and Hf are chemically almost indistinguishable and have to be separated by very fine techniques (typically ion-exchange chromatography). They are sold side by side. Hafnium controls in nuclear reactors depend on this.
items.why: Down-group similarity is taught; lateral similarity caused by f-shell shielding is a hidden consequence of the periodic table's full structure.
